top_picks.name: Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and today tested that idea properly. VOO holds the 500 largest US companies for a rock-bottom 0.03% fee. At the close the S&P 500 was down 1.52% to 7,316 and the Nasdaq Composite down 1.74%, its close now more than 10% below its record. That is a real down day, not the rounding error the intraday tape suggested. But look at the spread underneath it: the semiconductor ETF SMH fell 4.79%, SOXX fell 5.38%, Vertiv fell 17.26% on 4.6 times normal volume, Nebius fell 12.65%, KLA fell 10.8% and Micron fell 9.94%, while healthcare fell 0.61% and dividend value fell 0.18%. Owning all 500 meant you took a 1.5% loss instead of a 5% to 17% one. VOO now sits at the bottom of its 30-day range and about 2.1% below its 50-day average, which is an ordinary place to keep buying rather than a place to stop.
top_picks.why_now: Because the fastest way to have missed today was to have been sitting in cash waiting for clarity. A week ago 39 of 62 names closed at 30-day lows and a September hike arrived as a genuine threat. Today the S&P proxy is at a record. Nothing about the macro risk actually resolved (the hike is still priced near 65% to 80% odds, the 10-year is at about 4.75%), the market simply reversed on an oil headline. VOO is the position that does not require you to call any of that correctly.
top_picks.risk: A record high with a live September rate hike is the risk. If the Aug 12 CPI print runs hot, or the Hormuz deal that drove today's oil drop falls apart, the same index that rallied 1.5% today gives it back quickly. VOO is also about a third mega-cap technology now, so it is less diversified against an AI unwind than it looks: a genuine AI de-rating would take the core down with it, just by less.
sources: Nasdaq 100 enters correction, S&P 500 falls after Fed decision
Market indexes tumble on geopolitical tensions and chip stock selloff

grade.note: Unchanged at the top, and August opens by proving the point again. VOO is at a record and at the very top of its 30-day range, which means the boring core captured this snap-back without you having had to guess which corner of the AI chain would bounce first. Best Sharpe of the three at plain market risk, the lowest drawdown, a 13.3% ten-year CAGR, and roughly 23% odds of a down year. The one caveat is that a record high is a worse entry than a flush, so this is a keep-buying-on-schedule holding, not an all-at-once one, especially with a September hike live.

top_picks.bear_case: The whole index falls 20% to 35% in a genuine bear market (it did about -32% across 2020 and 2022). The specific risk right now: because a third of the S&P is mega-cap tech and that buildout is increasingly financed with debt, a September Fed hike plus a capex disappointment is a double hit the index cannot diversify away. Today was a preview, with the index down 1.5% purely on AI-complex weakness. If the market decides the buildout is spending far ahead of revenue, the index follows the chips down rather than shrugging them off. The Monte Carlo 5th-percentile one-year outcome is about -15%, and a 2022-style year is closer to -25% to -32%. The saving grace: it has always recovered given time, which is exactly why you dollar-cost-average rather than lump in.

competitors.name: VTI
competitors.note: Near-identical rival: total US market at the same 0.03% fee, adds mid and small caps for a touch more diversification. A coin-flip alternative.

competitors.name: SPY / IVV / SPLG
competitors.note: Same S&P 500 index. SPY is the most liquid (best for options) but costs 0.09%; IVV and SPLG match VOO on cost.

competitors.name: SCHD
competitors.note: The defensive alternative: a dividend-value basket that fell only 0.18% today and closed at the very top of its 30-day range, about 4.6% above its 50-day. Less AI concentration, more income, lower expected long-run return. A complement to VOO rather than a replacement.

top_picks.factors: Political: broad exposure to every policy at once, so it is the least policy-fragile holding on the board, though an oil-driven inflation scare and a hawkish Fed hit it like everything else. Environmental and structural: about a third of the index is mega-cap tech tied to the AI and data-center buildout, so it rides that electrification tailwind but carries its concentration risk. Today showed the sharper edge of that, where a supplier-layer flush was large enough to pull the whole index down 1.5% even though Alphabet closed higher.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: The quant levels are built from volatility, not opinion. Entry near the current 696 area sits just above the 50-day (685) and well above the 200-day (644), which is what an uptrend is supposed to look like. The stop near 619 is roughly 11% down, wide on purpose so ordinary noise does not knock you out of a core holding, and the take-profit near 888 gives about 2.5 to 1. For a buy-and-hold core the honest use of these numbers is not the stop, it is the reminder that an 11% drawdown here is normal and not a reason to sell.

top_picks.name: Eli Lilly
top_picks.thesis: You asked me to flag a good pharma buy when one shows up, and healthcare is now the only real leadership left on the board. The healthcare basket XLV fell just 0.61% today, sits at 89% of its 30-day range and about 6.8% above its 50-day average, on a session when 19 watchlist names logged heavy institutional liquidation and 39 closed at their 30-day lows. Underneath it, AbbVie closed higher, Novo Nordisk rose 1.22%, and both sit at the very top of their 30-day ranges alongside Johnson & Johnson at 92% and Merck at 87%. Lilly is the highest-quality business in that group. It owns roughly 60% of the obesity and GLP-1 market, and its biggest policy overhang has cleared: Lilly agreed to cut the Medicare price of its GLP-1s to $245 a month and won a three-year exemption from the pharma tariffs that otherwise hit patented drugs at a 100% rate starting Jul 31. Lilly fell only 0.87% today and still sits about 6.0% above its 50-day, so the trend is intact but the entry is not a discount.
top_picks.why_now: Because it is cheap in attention terms right now. On a day when money stampeded into optics and chips, healthcare was left behind, and that is usually when you get to add to a compounder without paying up. The known policy overhang is on the calendar rather than a surprise: CMS has selected 15 drugs for the third negotiation cycle (the first ever to include Part B drugs), comments close Aug 17 and any negotiated prices do not take effect until January 2028.
top_picks.risk: Valuation is the main one: a rich multiple leaves no room for a trial disappointment or a competitor surprise in obesity drugs. Policy is the second: the third Medicare negotiation cycle is live through 2026 and now reaches Part B drugs for the first time, and pharmaceutical tariffs remain an open question for prices not yet negotiated. Third, on days like today it simply will not keep up, and that is the cost of owning the defensive sleeve.
sources: Preparing for the July 31 pharma tariff deadline
Medicare opens GLP-1 access at a $50 monthly cap

grade.note: Held at A-, and today is exactly the trade-off you accept for owning it. Healthcare was one of only two groups on the whole board that failed to rally (XLV down 0.2% while semis rose 5%), and UnitedHealth and AbbVie are pinned at the bottom of their 30-day ranges. That is what a 0.6 beta looks like on a risk-on day: it lags the melt-ups and it cushions the flushes. The business case is unchanged, with a 30.4% ten-year CAGR, the best risk-reward of the three at about 4.9 to 1, and roughly 19% odds of a down year. Marked below a straight A for a rich valuation and the Medicare negotiation cycle now running through 2026.

top_picks.bear_case: Two real threats. Policy: Medicare negotiation round two (average 44% cuts, effective 2027) could squeeze margins across the industry once the current tariff exemption lapses in 2029. Competition and valuation: at about 32x you are priced for continued dominance, so any share loss to Novo's pill, a safety signal, or a manufacturing hiccup in the GLP-1 ramp hits a premium multiple hard. The simulation's 5th-percentile one-year outcome is about -20%, worse than VOO's, because a single stock carries single-name risk the ETF diversifies away. The cushions: about 60% GLP-1 share, a 31% long-run growth rate, a 107% ROE, and a 0.6 beta that softens broad selloffs.

competitors.name: ABBV (AbbVie)
competitors.note: The value-plus-income alternative: cheaper (PEG ~1.35), a dividend raised for 50-plus straight years, and an even lower beta. It closed green today at the very top of its 30-day range and 11.4% above its 50-day, so it is extended, but it is the better pure-income play.

competitors.name: NVO (Novo Nordisk)
competitors.note: The cheaper GLP-1 number two (roughly 16x versus Lilly's 32x, about 40% share). It rose 1.22% today and is also at the top of its range, so the deep-value gap has narrowed. Lilly keeps taking share and is still the quality pick.

competitors.name: XLV / MRK / JNJ
competitors.note: XLV is the hands-off basket (owns all of them at 0.09%) and fell only 0.61% today. Merck is cheap (~15x, 3% yield) but faces the 2028 Keytruda patent cliff; JNJ is the diversified sleep-well AAA name with less upside.

top_picks.factors: Political: drug-pricing policy has turned friendlier for Lilly specifically (the $245 Medicare price, the $50-a-month Medicare Bridge copay, and a tariff exemption running to 2029), leaving the 2027 Medicare negotiation round as the main residual risk. Environmental and structural: an aging, higher-weight population is a decade-long demand tailwind for obesity and diabetes drugs that runs independent of the economic cycle, the AI-capex cycle and the oil price, which is the single biggest reason to own healthcare at all in a week like this one.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: Entry around 1121 sits about 2.4% below the 50-day and 9.3% above the 200-day, which is the definition of a pullback inside an uptrend rather than a breakdown. The stop near 985 and the take-profit near 1791 produce the best risk-reward on the board at about 4.9 to 1. The Monte Carlo puts roughly 19% odds of a loss over one year and a median gain around 30%, with a worst modelled case near a 22% drawdown at the 5th percentile, so size it expecting a bad year to look like that, not like a wipeout.

top_picks.name: VanEck Semiconductor ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and semiconductors are the beating heart of your AI-infrastructure thesis. SMH holds the 25 biggest chip names (Nvidia, TSMC, Broadcom, AMD, ASML, Micron and the rest) in one 0.35% fund, so you own the layer without guessing which chip wins the next socket. That layer is now in an outright liquidation. SMH fell 4.79% today on 1.5 times normal volume, has logged 11 distribution days and two heavy-volume selloff events, closed at the very bottom of its 30-day range, and sits about 15.5% below its 50-day average and 20% below its 30-day high. Its own volatility reading has jumped to 45.5% annualized against a 33.5% median, so the fund's regime has flipped from normal to elevated volatility. The counterintuitive part still holds: the hyperscalers that BUY these chips keep raising budgets, with combined 2026 capex around $725 billion, up roughly 77% year over year. The order book is growing while the stocks fall.
top_picks.why_now: Because the demand evidence keeps improving faster than the price. DRAM spot prices are up roughly 700% year over year, SK Hynix is sold out of HBM, DRAM and NAND for 2026, Micron has exited consumer memory to serve AI customers, and three of the four hyperscalers raised capital-spending guidance in the last reporting round. The honest caveat is timing: you are buying after a 5% single-day bounce, not into the flush, and that bounce was not confirmed by volume.
top_picks.risk: Volume is the immediate one. A 5% sector rally on roughly half of average volume is short-covering as much as accumulation, and short-covering rallies fail more often than they extend. Underneath, the group still carries real damage: nine distribution days, 8.5% below its 50-day, SanDisk 24.6% below its 50-day with eleven distribution days. And the memory pricing that is powering the thesis is also raising costs for the hyperscalers who buy the chips, which is one reason Microsoft tied about $25 billion of its 2026 capex to component prices.
sources: Goldman says hedge funds sell US tech stocks at record pace
Nasdaq semiconductor stocks lead tech sell-off as memory chip crisis deepens

grade.note: Upgraded from C+ on the Jul 29 flush, but deliberately not further. What has changed is that the thesis got louder while the price was falling: memory is sold out for 2026, hyperscaler capex is now guided near $725 billion for the year (up 77%), and the whole chip complex rallied 5.1% today with SOXX up 6.4%. The technical repair has started too, with distribution days falling from 11 to 9. What holds the grade back is that today's bounce came on light volume (SMH traded barely half its average), it is still 8.5% below its 50-day, and its risk-reward has compressed from about 4.1 to 1 at the lows to 3.0 to 1 here. The best prices were last week. Keep scaling in on weakness rather than chasing green candles.

top_picks.bear_case: The AI-capex cycle could be over-building just as the memory squeeze breaks the consumer end of the market. DRAM spot prices are up sharply over the past year and roughly 93% of the big three's combined output has shifted to high-bandwidth memory for AI, which is why smartphone volumes are forecast to fall about 13% this year and PCs about 11%. That is a real demand hole opening underneath the AI boom. Add custom silicon challenging Nvidia's position, China building its own supply chain, hyperscaler free cash flow compressing (Meta's net income fell 14% while expenses rose 55%), and a buildout increasingly funded with debt just as the Fed flirts with a hike. It is concentrated and high-beta, so a market-wide risk-off takes it down harder than the index, and past cycles saw about -45% peak-to-trough. The simulation's 5th-percentile one-year outcome is about -20% and the worst path is far uglier. The offset: committed capex is still rising toward $725 billion and a trend-exit discipline historically sidesteps the worst of the drawdown.

competitors.name: SOXX
competitors.note: The near-identical rival (30 chip names, 0.35% fee). It fell harder today, down 5.38% on 1.81x volume and 18.2% below its 50-day. SMH is more concentrated in NVDA and TSM; SOXX spreads a touch wider. A coin-flip alternative.

competitors.name: VGT / QQQM
competitors.note: Own semis inside a broader tech basket: VGT fell 2.41% and QQQM 2.02% today against SMH's 4.79%, so you get lower single-sector risk and less volatility, but diluted exposure to the chip theme. The calmer way in while the memory-and-ROI question is unresolved.

competitors.name: NVDA
competitors.note: The single-name way to concentrate: NVDA fell 3.55% today, less than the fund, and sits at the bottom of its 30-day range but only 8.2% below its 50-day. You take on socket-loss and custom-silicon risk the ETF diversifies away.

top_picks.factors: Political: export controls on advanced chips to China cut both ways, and China's domestic push is now a direct competitive pressure rather than a distant threat. Environmental and structural: semiconductors sit at the top of the AI buildout and customer capex guides are still rising, which is why the demand case survives a tape this ugly, but the memory shortage has become a structural cost problem for the consumer electronics that used to underwrite the industry's volume. The near-term swing factor is the rate path, because this is the longest-duration equity exposure on the board.
top_picks.trade_reasoning: Entry near 545 is 8.5% below the 50-day, so you are still buying below trend, which is the good news. The stop near 434 is a wide 20%, which tells you the truth about this holding: it is a high-volatility position with a 44.5% maximum historical drawdown, and it needs to be sized so a 20% move against you is survivable. Take-profit near 882 gives about 3.0 to 1, down from 4.1 to 1 last week purely because the price rose. The Monte Carlo still shows the lowest one-year loss odds of the three at about 18%.

top_picks_note: Not a buy list, a research shortlist. August opens with the same three names as July, because a month boundary is a reason to re-examine the picks, not a reason to churn them: one diversified core (VOO), one quality healthcare compounder outside the AI theme (LLY), and one diversified way to own the AI hardware layer (SMH), whose grade goes back up to B- now that the thesis has been reinforced by sold-out memory and record hyperscaler capex while the technical damage slowly repairs. Two things were seriously considered for the third slot and deliberately passed over, for opposite reasons. Photonics is the best story on the board today, but a 14% average one-day jump on a policy headline is precisely the kind of move this page refuses to chase, so it goes on the board as a new section instead of into the picks. Established nuclear infrastructure is the more interesting candidate: it was the only group that fell today, the regulated fleet owners are pinned at the bottom of their 30-day ranges, and the contracts underneath (Constellation's 20-year Meta deal at Clinton, Talen's 1.9 gigawatt Amazon expansion through 2042) are already signed. It is a strong candidate for the next slot if the weakness persists, and it now has ten names on Sheet 1 to choose from rather than five. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy today.

insights.title: The selling stopped, but this rally is not being confirmed by volume
insights.body: The picture flipped completely from a week ago, when 39 of 62 names closed at 30-day lows. Today only three names on the whole board sit at the bottom of their 30-day range (Entergy, UnitedHealth and AbbVie) and twelve sit at the very top. The problem is what the volume says about who is doing the buying. Most of the biggest gainers traded below their own average volume: Fabrinet rose 16.63% on 0.97 times average volume, Lumentum 9.42% on 0.97x, Credo 9.31% on 0.77x, Intel 9.58% on 0.80x, SanDisk 10.14% on 0.89x, Micron 7.96% on 0.91x, AMD 8.14% on 0.87x and KLA 6.50% on 0.82x. The semiconductor ETF SMH rose 5.12% on just 0.55 times its average volume. Rallies that large on volume that thin are usually short-covering and a shortage of sellers rather than institutions accumulating. The genuine heavy-volume moves were narrower and more specific: Palantir up 26.59% on 1.73x volume after earnings, CoreWeave up 6.75% on 1.75x, Applied Optoelectronics up 20.86% on 1.38x, Microsoft up 2.01% on 1.81x. And the single clearest heavy-volume move on the board went the other way: Amazon fell 2.12% on 2.00 times average volume while sitting at the top of its 30-day range, which is what distribution into strength looks like. Twenty-four of the 70 names still carry a heavy liquidation event in their trailing window, and the distribution-day counts remain elevated where the damage was worst: SanDisk 11, Oracle 10, TSMC 9, Cameco 9, Intel 8, WESCO 8, PSEG 8.
insights.matters: For a long-term investor the useful signal is not the size of a one-day bounce, it is whether real money is behind it. Light-volume rallies can and do keep running, but they retrace far more often than heavy-volume ones, so this is not the day to rush a large purchase. Scale in on schedule, and note that the two names with the heaviest volume behind them today told opposite stories: Palantir bought aggressively on results, Amazon sold aggressively at the highs.
sources: Stock Market Today (Aug. 4, 2026): S&P 500 jumps as Palantir surges, oil slides

insights.title: A proposed ban on Chinese optical modules lit up the entire optics chain, and the board now has a photonics section
insights.body: The single biggest move on the board came from a policy headline. The administration is drafting rules, with the FCC leading, that would bar US data centers from importing next-generation Chinese-made optical transceiver modules on national-security grounds. Every US-listed optics name repriced instantly: Applied Optoelectronics up 20.86%, Fabrinet up 16.63%, Coherent up 14.56%, Lumentum up 9.42%, Credo up 9.31%, Corning up 7.48% and Ciena up 6.27%. The new Photonics and Optical Interconnect group averaged a 14.16% gain, the best of any section on either sheet, on a day when the next best was memory at 7.33%. The structural story underneath the headline is real and predates it: light, not electricity, is how data now moves between GPU clusters, optics content rises with every hardware generation as 800G gives way to 1.6T, and LightCounting sizes the AI-cluster optics market at $16.5 billion in 2025 going to $26 billion in 2026, roughly 60% growth in a single year. Applied Optoelectronics has shipped its first volume 800G transceivers to a hyperscale customer and has floated a path past $1 billion of revenue. Because you asked for it, photonics is now its own section (06) on Sheet 1, holding Coherent, Lumentum, Fabrinet, Applied Optoelectronics and Credo, with the slower-moving glass and long-haul names (Corning, Ciena) split out into their own Fiber Optics and Cabling group above it.
insights.matters: This is a good long-term theme having a bad-habit kind of day. The demand growth is genuine and it sits at the exact bottleneck of the AI build-out, which is why it earns a permanent place on the board. But a 20% single-day move on a draft regulation is not an entry point, and the valuations reflect it: Applied Optoelectronics trades near 73 times forward earnings after a roughly 216% year-to-date run, and today's moves came largely on below-average volume. Nothing has been enacted yet, and trade rules of this kind are frequently softened. If you want this exposure, the lower-drama routes are the larger names in the section (Coherent, Fabrinet) bought in tranches on quiet days, or simply owning it inside a chip and AI-hardware basket such as SMH or SOXX, which hold the optical supply chain without asking you to pick the winner of a policy fight.
sources: Optical Communication Stocks Rally as Trump Administration Plans to Ban Chinese Modules
Lumentum, Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics surge on strong optical demand momentum tied to AI
Applied Optoelectronics and Coherent Gain 7%, Lumentum Adds 5% as Risk-On Feeling Spreads to Optics

insights.title: Oil collapsed on a Hormuz deal headline, which is the one thing that could take a September hike off the table
insights.body: A week ago the story was an oil shock forcing the Fed's hand. Today it partly reversed. Treasury Secretary Bessent said the US and Iran could reach an agreement as soon as this week to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, closed since April, and crude fell hard: WTI down about 3.2% near $77.77 and Brent down about 5.1% near $83.44, versus roughly $84 WTI at the Jul 29 peak. That matters because energy was the entire reason the Aug 12 CPI print became dangerous. The Fed's position has not changed yet: it held at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 in a 9-to-3 vote, its most divided since 2016, with Cleveland's Hammack, Minneapolis's Kashkari and Dallas's Logan all dissenting in favour of a hike, and markets still price roughly 65% to 80% odds of higher rates by September. The bond market is siding with the dissenters: the 10-year sits near 4.75%, up from about 4.48% a month ago, with the 2-year at 4.28%, leaving the 10Y-2Y curve positively sloped by about 0.47. Underneath the noise, inflation is still improving: June CPI 3.5% year over year (down from 4.2%), core 2.6% (down from 2.8%), unemployment 4.2%. Note the oil chip on the macro strip still reads $84.25 from Jul 27, because FRED publishes with a lag and has not caught today's drop.
insights.matters: Rates are the single biggest input to what your holdings are worth, because the 10-year is the yardstick everything else is priced against. The set-up into Aug 12 is now genuinely better than it was last week: falling oil feeds directly into a softer headline CPI, and a soft print takes the September hike back off the table. The risk is that the Hormuz deal is a headline, not a signature. If it falls through, oil and the hike odds both go straight back up. That two-sided risk is an argument for adding on a schedule rather than making one large bet before the print.
sources: Dow futures jump 600 points as Bessent says Strait of Hormuz deal imminent
Three Fed Dissenters Signal September Hike Is Live After Most Hawkish FOMC Vote in Nearly Ten Years
September Rate Hike Becomes Most Likely Outcome According To Markets

insights.title: The spenders are guiding to about $725 billion, and the market is paying the suppliers rather than the spenders
insights.body: Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta have now collectively guided 2026 capital spending to roughly $725 billion, up about 77% from last year's record $410 billion. The rough split is Amazon near $200 billion, Microsoft near $190 billion, Alphabet $175 to $185 billion and Meta $115 to $135 billion. Three of the four raised guidance in the latest reporting round; Amazon held only because it had already published its number in February. The reasons for the raises are worth reading closely, because they are not all demand: Meta cited component pricing and extra data-center costs, and Microsoft attributed roughly $25 billion of its 2026 figure to component prices, which is the memory shortage showing up in someone else's cost line. Investors have started to push back, and Alphabet fell about 7% on its own report. Today the split was visible in real time on the board: Amazon fell 2.12% on twice its average volume while Microsoft rose only 2.01%, and meanwhile their suppliers ripped, with servers and cooling up 7.13%, memory up 7.33% and photonics up 14.16%. Palantir was the day's exception among the large caps, up 26.59% on 1.73 times volume after beating and guiding fiscal 2026 revenue to about $7.65 billion.
insights.matters: This is the cleanest read on where the profit actually lands. When capital spending is accelerating, the money moves from the buyers' cash flow to the sellers' revenue, and the market is repricing accordingly. It also frames the central risk of the whole theme: capex of this size only stays up if the returns show up, and the hyperscalers' own margin commentary is where the first crack would appear. Owning both sides (the customers in section 09 and the suppliers in sections 01 through 07) is the practical hedge, which is one more argument for a broad basket over a single link in the chain.
sources: Google, Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon capex spending to hit $725 billion in 2026, up 77%
Amazon, Meta and Microsoft face skeptical investors after Google report sparked sell-off
US Stocks Hover Near Record Highs As Palantir Surges, Oil Drops On Iran Deal Hopes

insights.title: Memory has the strongest fundamentals and the worst chart on the board at the same time
insights.body: The memory shortage keeps getting more extreme. DRAM spot prices are up close to 700% over the past year, contract prices are set to rise 50% to 55% this quarter against the fourth quarter of 2025, and SK Hynix has said its HBM, DRAM and NAND capacity is essentially sold out for 2026. Micron has exited the consumer memory market entirely to concentrate on enterprise and AI customers. The 2026 supply-demand gaps for DRAM, NAND and HBM are running near 4.9%, 4.2% and 5.1%, the widest since 2011, and Bank of America models DRAM revenue up 51% and NAND up 45% this year. HBM stack pricing runs roughly $200 for HBM3, $300 for HBM3E and an estimated $500 for HBM4. Now put that against the board. Memory rose 7.33% today, the second-best group, and it is still the most technically damaged corner on Sheet 1: SanDisk gained 10.14% and remains 24.55% below its 50-day with eleven distribution days and two heavy liquidation events, and Micron gained 7.96% and remains 14.2% below its 50-day with seven distribution days. Both bounced on below-average volume.
insights.matters: This gap between excellent fundamentals and a broken chart is the most common situation a long-term investor actually faces, and it is uncomfortable by design. The fundamentals tell you the earnings are coming; the chart tells you institutions were still selling into that news as recently as last week. The reconciliation is usually time rather than a clean bottom. If you want the exposure, SOXX is the practical route because it holds Micron, SanDisk and Western Digital alongside Nvidia and AMD, which spares you from guessing which memory maker captures the cycle. SK Hynix, the HBM leader at roughly half the market, trades only in Seoul, so a basket is the only way most US investors touch it.
sources: DRAM and NAND prices jump as Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron tighten supply
Samsung warns of memory shortages driving industry-wide price surge in 2026
2026 Market Outlook: SK hynix's HBM to Fuel AI Memory Boom

insights.title: Nuclear infrastructure was the only group that fell today, while its contracts keep getting longer
insights.body: On a day when thirteen of fifteen groups rallied and semiconductors rose 5%, established nuclear and power was the one that went backwards, averaging a 0.95% decline. Vistra fell 7.31%, Constellation 3.27% and Talen 2.86%, and the regulated fleet owners are sitting at the floor of their recent ranges: Dominion, Southern and PSEG are all at the very bottom of their 30-day range and Entergy is at 5%, with PSEG carrying eight distribution days and Entergy seven. The stated reason is a rotation rather than a nuclear problem: money is questioning how fast AI capital spending converts to profit and is moving out of the power-and-payback trade into the hardware names that are visibly shipping product, with Vistra's Aug 7 earnings adding a reason to wait. What did not change is the contracted revenue underneath. Constellation's 20-year deal with Meta supplies 1.1 gigawatts from Clinton starting in 2027 and keeps a plant that was slated to close running to 2047. Talen expanded its Amazon agreement to as much as 1.9 gigawatts through at least 2042. Across the industry, 13 announced projects now commit more than 9.8 gigawatts of nuclear capacity to data centers. Uranium disagreed with the power names entirely: Cameco rose 4.45%, the URA basket 4.04% and Centrus 2.31%. Because you like the nuclear names that already own infrastructure, section 08 has been widened from five names to ten, adding Talen, Dominion, Southern (which built Vogtle, the only new US reactors this century), PSEG and Entergy alongside Constellation, Vistra, Cameco, BWX Tech and GE Vernova.
insights.matters: This is the mirror image of the photonics card, and it is the more interesting one for a buy-and-hold investor. Photonics went up 14% on a headline; nuclear infrastructure went down on sentiment while its cash flows got contractually longer. Weakness in businesses whose revenue is locked in for two decades is the kind of setup worth accumulating into, not away from. The valuation spread inside the group is wide and worth knowing: Talen trades near 11.7 times forward earnings, Vistra and PSEG near 16.9, Dominion 18.7, Southern 20.2, Constellation 22.6. The merchant operators (Constellation, Vistra, Talen) carry the upside and the power-price risk; the regulated utilities (Dominion, Southern, PSEG, Entergy) pay dividends and earn a regulated return, which is why they move less in both directions. Vistra reports Aug 7, so expect noise. For a single diversified holding, NLR is the utility-heavy nuclear basket and URA is the purer uranium-miner version.
sources: Vistra slides as AI-power names weaken and no fresh company catalyst emerges
Every Nuclear-Powered Data Center Deal: Google, Amazon, Meta & Microsoft (2026)
Beyond the Hype: Assessing Hyperscaler Nuclear Commitments Against U.S. Energy Realities

insights.title: Healthcare sat out the rally, and the third Medicare negotiation round is the calendar item to track
insights.body: Healthcare was the only other group besides nuclear power to finish lower, with the XLV basket down 0.2% while technology rose nearly 4%. UnitedHealth fell 1.77% and sits at 4% of its 30-day range, AbbVie fell 0.61% at 5% of its range, and Johnson & Johnson fell 0.75%. This is ordinary rotation: on a strong risk-on day the defensive sleeve is the funding source. The policy calendar is the part worth actually tracking. CMS has selected 15 more drugs for the third cycle of Medicare drug price negotiation, and for the first time the list includes drugs paid under Part B rather than Part D alone. Negotiations run through 2026, public comments on the proposed rule close Aug 17, CMS expects to finalise in the autumn, and any resulting prices do not take effect until January 1, 2028. For context on magnitude, the first round produced negotiated prices 38% to 79% below prior prices, with CMS projecting about $6 billion of net first-year savings. Pharmaceutical tariffs remain a separate open question, and are expected to affect prices not yet negotiated rather than those already settled.
insights.matters: Healthcare is on this board specifically as the reminder that good businesses exist outside the AI trade, and today shows the trade-off in both directions: it did not fall when the AI chain was being liquidated last week, and it did not rise when the AI chain rebounded today. That is the job it is doing. The policy overhang is real but it is scheduled, dated and partly priced, which is very different from a surprise. For a diversified holding XLV covers pharma, insurers and devices in one line; for a single name Eli Lilly remains the growth-plus-defense pick on this board, with the understanding that a rich multiple leaves little room for disappointment.
sources: CMS Announces Selection of Drugs for Third Cycle of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program
CMS Issues First Proposed Rule for IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation
Key Facts About Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

smart_money.intro: Where the large, well-informed pools of money are actually positioned, read from the three sources a private investor can legitimately see: weekly CFTC futures positioning, published reports of Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage flow (the desk data itself is proprietary, so this is press reporting rather than a primary feed), and disclosed policy and corporate spending. It is a timing signal, not a guarantee, and institutions are wrong regularly. Treat it as context for when to add to a position you already believe in, never as the reason to own it.

items.title: Goldman's desk: the record tech exit has turned, and net tech longs just posted their biggest jump in five years
items.body: Reported Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage data describes a full round trip in about six weeks. Through mid-July, hedge funds sold US technology at a record pace, acting as net sellers in six of eight weeks with a cumulative reduction near 10% of market value, the largest retreat since the series began more than a decade ago. Semiconductors led the outflows, exposure to the mega-cap tech complex fell to its lowest point of the year, and the money that left rotated into commercial services, staples, real estate, energy and broad index products. Late in July, as AI stocks fell hard, major banks including Goldman began issuing additional collateral calls to hedge funds whose books were concentrated in the sector, which is the mechanical part of a de-grossing. Goldman also disclosed that as of Jun 30 roughly 16% of its prime exposure was tied to AI memory-related names. The more recent reporting points the other way: net long exposure to global information technology has posted its biggest increase in more than five years, with positioning back near the highest levels since the bank began tracking in 2016.
items.matters: This is the missing explanation for why a 5% chip rally can happen on half the normal volume. When leveraged books have already been forced down to their lowest exposure of the year, there is very little supply left to sell, and prices can rise sharply without heavy buying. The flip side is the warning: if positioning is already being rebuilt toward record levels, the cushion that made this bounce easy is being spent. Fast re-leveraging is what makes the next shock sharp again, so treat strength here as a chance to add gradually, not to concentrate.
sources: Goldman Sachs (GS) Says Hedge Funds Made Their Biggest US Tech Exit Yet
Wall Street Rushes to Issue Margin Calls as AI Stocks Plunge
Hedge funds boost tech bets to record highs on AI optimism: Goldman Sachs

items.title: Leveraged funds covered equity shorts, pressed their bet against bonds, and sold volatility
items.body: The CFTC's Jul 28 report, released Jul 31, updates the picture that had been frozen for two weeks. In S&P 500 e-mini futures, asset managers stayed heavily net long at 944,770 contracts (47.6% of open interest) and added 15,611 on the week, while leveraged funds remained net short at 297,476 but bought back 25,389 contracts of that short. The same pattern is clearer in the Nasdaq-100, where leveraged funds cut their net short by 16,392 contracts to 58,298 while asset managers added 4,134. In the 10-year Treasury note the two sides are at their most extreme: asset managers are net long 2,611,964 contracts and leveraged funds are net short 2,155,739, and the leveraged side added another 90,934 contracts to that short during the week, a direct bet that yields go higher. In VIX futures, leveraged funds increased their net short by 15,387 contracts, a bet that volatility stays low.
items.matters: Read the three together and the fast money is positioned for exactly the tape it got: cover the equity shorts, stay short bonds, sell volatility. That combination has been correct so far, with the 10-year at 4.75% and the VIX near 15.9. It is also a crowded and fragile combination, because all three legs lose at once if the Aug 12 CPI print surprises in either direction hard enough to move rates fast. Remember the lag: this data was collected Jul 28, before both the Hormuz headline and today's rally, so it describes where the money was, not where it is.
sources: CFTC Traders in Financial Futures, week of Jul 28, 2026

items.title: Policy is now the biggest single-day driver on the board, and it moved optics, oil and drugs at once
items.body: Three separate policy threads moved money today. First, the draft rule barring Chinese-made next-generation optical transceivers from US data centers, with the FCC leading, repriced the entire optics chain by 6% to 21% in a session and is the direct cause of the best-performing group on the board. Second, the Treasury Secretary's comment that a Strait of Hormuz agreement could be reached within days knocked roughly 3% off WTI and 5% off Brent, which does more for the September rate decision than any Fed speech this week. Third, CMS moved the third round of Medicare drug price negotiation forward, reaching Part B drugs for the first time, with comments closing Aug 17. Alongside these, the standing government positions on the board have not changed: Washington holds equity in Intel, MP Materials and Lithium Americas, and is the anchor customer for Centrus, BWX Technologies, Rocket Lab and Palantir. Those GOV-badged names were broadly strong today, with Intel up 9.58%, MP Materials up 7.73% and Palantir up 26.59%.
items.matters: Policy as a moat cuts both ways, and today was the pleasant direction. An import ban on a foreign competitor hands domestic suppliers pricing power they did not earn commercially, which is genuinely valuable while it lasts and can be reversed by the same pen that wrote it. The practical discipline is to treat a policy-driven jump as a reason to review a position, never as the thesis itself. A business that only works because of a draft regulation is a bet on politics; one that would work anyway and gets helped by the regulation is an investment.
sources: Optical Communication Stocks Rally as Trump Administration Plans to Ban Chinese Modules
Dow futures jump 600 points as Bessent says Strait of Hormuz deal imminent
CMS Announces Selection of Drugs for Third Cycle of Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program

items.title: About $725 billion of committed spending is the floor under every supplier on Sheet 1
items.body: The four largest buyers of AI infrastructure have guided 2026 capital spending to roughly $725 billion between them, up about 77% from $410 billion last year, with Amazon near $200 billion, Microsoft near $190 billion, Alphabet $175 to $185 billion and Meta $115 to $135 billion. Three of the four raised in the most recent round. Two details matter more than the headline number. The first is composition: Meta pointed to component pricing and additional data-center costs, and Microsoft tied about $25 billion of its figure specifically to component prices, meaning a meaningful slice of the increase is memory inflation rather than extra capacity. The second is the market's reaction: Alphabet fell about 7% on its report and Amazon fell 2.12% on double average volume today at the top of its range, while the companies selling into that budget rose 5% to 14%.
items.matters: For a long-term holder this is the most concrete number on the whole page, because it is committed spending rather than a forecast, and it is what turns into revenue for the chip, memory, server, optics, electrical and power names on Sheet 1. It is also the number to watch for the first sign of trouble: the theme does not break when a supplier misses, it breaks when a hyperscaler cuts this figure. Nobody has cut. Until someone does, weakness in the suppliers is more likely to be positioning than a change in demand.
sources: Big Tech's $725B AI Capex in 2026, Up 77% From 2025
Amazon, Meta and Microsoft face skeptical investors after Google report sparked sell-off

primer.intro: A large AI data center is a machine built in physical layers, and money flows into it from the top (the customers who order it) down through every supplier who makes a piece. Here is where the dollars land, and why the least glamorous layers can be the safest way to invest.

sections.h: Start at the top: the customers
sections.p: The hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle) announce the giant spending budgets, now roughly $725B in 2026, that everyone else competes to capture. Owning them is the most diversified way to own the theme, because their core businesses (ads, cloud, software) fund the AI bet and keep earning even if AI spending pauses. Two cautions surfaced this quarter: the market now scrutinizes the return on that capex (Alphabet raised its 2026 spend and its free cash flow turned negative, and Meta's net income fell 14% while expenses rose 55%), and the group is increasingly tapping external financing, which makes the whole chain more rate-sensitive.

Nvidia (NVDA) designs the GPUs that do the AI math; AMD (AMD) is the challenger; Broadcom (AVGO) builds the custom chips hyperscalers increasingly design in-house, a trend now challenging Nvidia's near-monopoly. None own factories: TSMC (TSM) prints the chips using machines only ASML (ASML) makes, and every GPU needs memory from Micron (MU). Highest growth, highest risk, and the layer that falls first on any overcapacity or competition scare.

Memory deserves its own line now. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron control over 95% of global DRAM and have shifted roughly 93% of combined output to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. That has sent AI memory pricing sharply higher and left consumer-grade memory scarce, which is why smartphone volumes are forecast to fall about 13% this year and PCs about 11%. It is a margin tailwind for MU, SNDK and WDC and a cost shock for every device maker, and it makes this the most cyclical layer of the whole buildout. SK Hynix is Seoul-listed, so US investors reach it mainly through the baskets.

sections.h: Layer 2: The box and the room
sections.p: The chips get assembled into servers by Super Micro (SMCI) and Dell (DELL). A rack of AI chips runs blazing hot, so it needs advanced cooling and power distribution from Vertiv (VRT), and fast switches from Arista (ANET) to connect racks together. This is the guts of the room, and Vertiv's 17% single-day drop after a raised guide is a reminder that these are project businesses whose revenue lands unevenly quarter to quarter.

AI splits one job across thousands of chips, so they must talk at the speed of light over fiber. Transceivers and lasers come from Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE), long-haul interconnect from Ciena (CIEN), and the actual glass fiber from Corning (GLW). Optics content rises with every hardware generation, though these names trade with the chip complex on risk-off days and have been among the hardest hit in this drawdown.

The least glamorous and often most attractive layer: switchgear from Eaton (ETN) and Hubbell (HUBB), the steel and PVC conduit that carries every wire from Atkore (ATKR), jobsite supply from WESCO (WCC), transmission and substation build from Quanta (PWR), and the raw steel from Nucor (NUE). Physical, hard-to-substitute, multi-year backlogs. This layer had held up through most of the AI selloff, so heavy institutional selling arriving here is worth watching as a signal about the pace of the buildout itself.

A data center is useless without electricity, and AI has made power the true bottleneck. Existing-reactor operators signing long deals are Constellation (CEG) and Vistra (VST); fuel comes from Cameco (CCJ); reactor and SMR technology from BWX (BWXT), Oklo (OKLO) and NuScale (SMR); and near-term gas-turbine and grid power from GE Vernova (GEV). The operators have generally held up better than the developers, because they sell electricity today while the developers are selling a milestone in 2028.

Follow a dollar of capex: it lands most heavily on the chip layer, which captures the most dollars but carries the most risk (a rival can win a socket, custom silicon can erode the moat, and an overcapacity or return-on-investment scare hits it first). The power, conduit, cooling and fiber layers are lower-binary: whatever chip and model win, the building still needs steel, copper, transformers and megawatts. That is the trade-off, highest upside in silicon, more durable margins of safety in the infrastructure beneath it, though this week showed that in a broad de-grossing everything sells together for a while.

macro_strategy.regime_label: Risk-on reversal on an oil headline, with a September hike still live and the rally running on thin volume
macro_strategy.regime_detail: The regime flipped from the Jul 29 flush, and the quant model now reads the market as an uptrend at normal volatility rather than the elevated-volatility state it showed last week. Three forces define the tape. First, energy relief: Treasury Secretary Bessent said a Strait of Hormuz reopening deal could be signed within days, WTI fell about 3.2% toward $78 and Brent about 5.1%, unwinding the oil shock that made the Aug 12 CPI print dangerous. Second, the Fed has not moved with it: the Jul 29 hold at 3.50-3.75% came on a 9-to-3 vote with three presidents dissenting for a hike, the most divided decision since 2016, September hike odds remain roughly 65% to 80%, and the 10-year has pushed to about 4.75% against a 2-year at 4.28%. The bond market is not buying the all-clear even as stocks make records. Third, the rally's internals are thin: semiconductors rose 5.12% on 0.55 times average volume, and most of the largest single-name gains came on below-average volume, which is the signature of short-covering into an empty book rather than institutions accumulating. Underlying inflation continues to improve (June CPI 3.5% from 4.2%, core 2.6% from 2.8%, unemployment 4.2%), so this remains an energy-and-positioning story layered on genuine disinflation, not a return of broad inflation.

drivers.reading: Hawkish hold with a live hike. Fed funds 3.50-3.75%, held on a 9-to-3 vote with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissenting for a hike, and September priced near 65% to 80% odds of higher rates. The 10-year at about 4.75% is up from roughly 4.48% a month ago, the 2-year is 4.28%, and the 10Y-2Y curve is positively sloped by about 0.47. CFTC data shows leveraged funds added 90,934 contracts to an already record 10-year short, so the fast money is pressing the higher-yields bet.
drivers.playbook: Stop assuming the next move is a cut, because three Fed presidents just voted against that assumption. A flat-to-higher path keeps pressure on anything valued on distant profits, which is why quantum, space, the neoclouds and pre-revenue nuclear stay sized as venture bets. It also means the 10-year at about 4.75% pays you a real return to be patient, so there is no penalty for adding in tranches instead of all at once. Dividend value (SCHD) and the regulated utilities in section 08 are the parts of the board that a higher-for-longer path hurts least on a cash-flow basis, even though they trade badly on rate spikes.

drivers.reading: Improving, and today the oil risk started to unwind. June CPI 3.5% year over year (down from 4.2%) and core 2.6% (down from 2.8%), both trending the right way. WTI is down about 3.2% near $78 on Hormuz reopening hopes after peaking near $84. The macro strip still shows $84.25 because FRED publishes with a lag. Aug 12 is the print that decides September, and cheaper crude is the single most helpful input it could have.
drivers.playbook: Do not press risk into the Aug 12 print in either direction. Cheaper crude is a genuine tailwind for the headline number and for the September decision, but it rests on a deal that has not been signed. Own some pricing power and real assets as the hedge: market-priced power operators (CEG, VST, TLN), healthcare that passes costs through (LLY, XLV), and broad exposure via VOO or VTI. Keep some cash available for the print itself rather than deploying everything before it.

drivers.reading: Still strong where it counts for this board. Unemployment 4.2% and steady. Hyperscaler capital spending guided to roughly $725 billion for 2026, up 77%, with three of four raising. Memory is sold out for the year, DRAM spot prices are up close to 700% year over year, and the AI-cluster optics market is growing about 60% this year. The demand side of the thesis is not the problem.
drivers.playbook: This is the leg of the thesis that is working, so let it work rather than trading around it. Anchor on the diversified core (VOO, VTI) and hold the AI hardware sleeve (SMH, SOXX) sized so a 30% to 45% drawdown is survivable, because that is what its history says it does. Memory and optics are where the demand evidence is strongest, and both are best owned through a basket rather than a single name given how violently the individual stocks move.

drivers.reading: The dominant driver right now, and the reason to be careful. Hedge funds cut US tech at a record pace into mid-July, took collateral calls late in the month, and have since posted their biggest increase in net technology exposure in more than five years. Leveraged funds covered 25,389 contracts of S&P shorts and 16,392 of Nasdaq shorts into Jul 28, and are short volatility. An empty book explains a big rally on light volume; a rebuilt book removes the cushion for next time.
drivers.playbook: Use flow as a timing input only. An emptied book explains why today was easy and argues against chasing; a rebuilt book argues for keeping dry powder. Practically: slow your purchases in whatever just ran hardest (photonics, high-multiple chips), and speed them up where price fell while the business improved (nuclear infrastructure). When leveraged funds are short bonds and short volatility at the same time, assume the next surprise gets amplified, and keep position sizes where a fast 10% move does not force you to act.

drivers.reading: Now a first-order market driver rather than background. A draft FCC-led ban on Chinese optical transceiver modules in US data centers moved the optics chain 6% to 21% in a single session. Medicare drug price negotiation entered its third cycle, reaching Part B drugs for the first time, with comments closing Aug 17 and prices effective 2028. Government equity stakes and anchor-customer relationships continue to underwrite Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas, Centrus, BWX Technologies, Rocket Lab and Palantir.
drivers.playbook: Let policy adjust your sizing, never form your thesis. A draft import ban is worth a review of what you own, not a purchase at a 20% premium the same morning. Prefer businesses that would work without the rule and get helped by it (Coherent, Fabrinet, Corning) over ones that only work because of it. The GOV-badged names (Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas, Centrus, BWX Tech, Rocket Lab, Palantir) carry a government floor under demand and the matching risk that an administration changes its mind, so keep them a slice rather than a concentration.

macro_strategy.positioning: The practical stance is unchanged from last week even though the tape reversed, and that consistency is the point: nothing about a two-session round trip should change a ten-year plan. Keep the diversified core (VOO or VTI) as the largest position and keep adding on schedule rather than in one lump at a record high. Treat today's strength as a reason to slow purchases in whatever ran hardest, not to speed them up: photonics rose 14% on a draft regulation and most of the chip complex rallied on half its normal volume, and neither is an entry point. Where the buying is genuinely more attractive is where prices fell while the business improved, and that is established nuclear infrastructure, the only group on the board that declined today, with regulated fleet owners at the bottom of their 30-day ranges and twenty-year hyperscaler contracts already signed underneath. Keep the defensive sleeve (LLY, XLV) that lagged today, because it is doing the job it was bought for. Keep speculative names on Sheet 2 sized as venture bets: they rose 4% to 7% today and will give it back just as fast. Hold cash for the Aug 12 CPI print rather than deploying it all before, and remember that the 10-year at 4.75% means a genuinely risk-free alternative still pays you to be patient.

scenarios.trigger: If the Hormuz deal is actually signed and the Aug 12 CPI print lands soft
scenarios.response: The September hike gets priced back out, the 10-year eases from 4.75% toward the mid-4s, and this rally broadens from short-covering into real buying. In that world the groups that are still below their 50-day have the most room: memory and chip equipment, the optics names once the policy froth settles, and the rate-sensitive utilities in section 08 that have been sold hardest. The mistake to avoid is waiting for confirmation and buying only after the move, which is what today punished.

scenarios.trigger: If the Hormuz talks collapse and oil goes back toward $90
scenarios.response: The Jul 29 tape returns quickly, and it returns to a market that has spent its cushion: positioning has been rebuilt, leveraged funds are short volatility, and the rally that got us here came on thin volume. Expect the sharpest damage in exactly what rose most today, photonics and the high-multiple chip names. The core, healthcare and the regulated utilities are what hold up. This is the scenario that rewards having added on a schedule rather than in one lump today.

scenarios.trigger: If the Fed hikes in September
scenarios.response: The long-duration parts of the board reprice first: quantum, space, the neoclouds and any name whose profits are mostly in the future. Anything valued on cash flow today holds better, which means the regulated utilities, healthcare and the dividend sleeve (SCHD). A hike would also confirm what the leveraged 10-year short has been betting, so expect the bond move to be quick. Nothing on this page should be sold in anticipation of it: a single 25 basis-point move does not change a decade-long thesis, it changes the price you pay this quarter.

scenarios.trigger: If a hyperscaler cuts its capital-spending guidance
scenarios.response: This is the one that actually matters, and it has not happened. Roughly $725 billion of committed 2026 spending is the floor under every supplier on Sheet 1, and the theme does not break when a supplier misses a quarter, it breaks when a buyer cuts the budget. Watch the hyperscalers' own margin commentary for the first sign. If that number ever comes down, reduce the single-name AI hardware exposure first and let the diversified core and healthcare carry the portfolio.

watchlist_notes: Two sheets, same columns. Sheet 1 is the established, large-dollar side and it now runs ten sections rather than nine: semis and fab, chip equipment, memory and storage, servers and cooling, fiber optics and cabling, the new photonics and optical interconnect group, electrical and steel, nuclear infrastructure and power majors, big tech, and healthcare. Sheet 2 is the smaller-dollar speculative side (nuclear developers and fuel, quantum, space and defense, government-backed materials and small AI infra, neoclouds). Two changes landed today at your request. First, photonics is now its own section (06) holding Coherent, Lumentum, Fabrinet, Applied Optoelectronics and Credo, with the slower glass-and-long-haul names, Corning and Ciena, split out above it into Fiber Optics and Cabling. Silicon-photonics micro-caps such as POET were left off deliberately: too small and too pre-revenue for a long-term sheet. Second, nuclear infrastructure (08) doubled from five names to ten, adding Talen, Dominion, Southern, PSEG and Entergy to Constellation, Vistra, Cameco, BWX Tech and GE Vernova, so the section now covers the merchant operators selling power straight to data centers and the regulated fleet owners that earn a rate-regulated return, not just the AI-power trade. Read the Bull Score first: it is six checks on whether the long-term case holds, and hovering it shows which checks passed. What the board looks like at midday: thirteen of fifteen groups are green, led by photonics at +14.16%, memory at +7.33%, space at +7.15% and servers at +7.13%, while nuclear infrastructure (-0.95%) and healthcare (-0.04%) are the only groups lower. Twelve names sit at the top of their 30-day range and only three at the bottom (Entergy, UnitedHealth, AbbVie), a near-complete reversal from Jul 29 when 39 of 62 closed at their lows. The caution flag is volume: most of the biggest gainers rose on below-average volume, and SMH gained 5.12% on just 0.55 times its average, so this is a short-covering rally until heavy volume confirms it. Distribution days remain elevated where the damage was worst (SanDisk 11, Oracle 10, TSMC 9, Cameco 9, Intel 8, WESCO 8, PSEG 8). Sheet 2 bounced hard, 4% to 7% across quantum, space and the neoclouds, which is what those names do in both directions: size them like venture bets, not positions.
